title: Viral Gene Editing and Bioinformatics Core for Institution # 269291
text: The overall objective of the Viral Gene Editing and Bioinformatics Core (VGEBC) is to provide basic and clinical researchers with knowledge and familiarity with the latest technology involving a genetic approach, including gene editing to investigate the neuroscience of HIV and exploring novel strategies for suppressing viral infection. The VGEBC will offer access to a comprehensive and integrated CRISPR gene editing design and implementation pipeline. Our collaborative, multi-institutional team of experts will provide guidance, training and shared resources allowing successful utilization of the CRISPR technology in projects focused on a better understanding of the mechanisms of neuroHIV and the discovery of reliable biomarkers for early diagnosis and development of intelligent therapies toward a cure. The services will include canonical DNA editors: SpCas9 and SaCas9, novel CasX and CasY, RNA editing Cas13, and CRISPR-mediated gene expression regulation using catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9) fused to a variety of effector domains. Additionally, the Core will test and implement new upgrades to existing and novel gene editors as they emerge from the literature. The design and selection of optimal gRNAs will be performed with the assistance of the co-director and his bioinformatics team. The Core's unique expertise in gene editing, bioinformatics sequence analysis, and gene delivery, and the cross- collaboration between two universities will be used to guide investigators in: i) the design of the most up-to-date and safe gene-editing techniques; ii) the utilization of the latest bioinformatic pipeline to maximize in target and minimize off-target effects; iii) the development strategies for activation or suppression of gene transcription; iv) the employment of the most accurate and cost-effective genomic sequencing with long-read technology. Our Core will work closely with the other cores of the CNHC to promote a comprehensive, synergistic, multidisciplinary collaborative program. Primary patient-derived cells will be available through the Clinical and Translational Research Support Core (CTRSC) in conjunction with the NeuroHIV Community Partnership Core (NHCPC); and cell lines and cell culture models will be available through the Cell Biology and Functional Analyses Core (CBFAC). Biostatistical support will be provided through the Central Administrative and Management Core (CAMC). We will provide expertise and services to pilot project awardees through interactions with the Developmental Research and Mentorship Core (DRMC). This synergistic approach will ensure the success of the CNHC developmental award recipients and users in conducting productive high-impact research in neuroHIV research.

title: Harnessing PRX1 expressing cells for endogenous periodontal regeneration
text:
In patients affected by periodontitis, after controlling the disease, periodontists and general dentists need to
perform regenerative procedures to re-establish the normal anatomy and function of the periodontium. However
current regenerative therapies are ineffective as they are unable to fully regenerate the missing periodontal
tissues. With the final goal of developing more effective periodontal regenerative therapies, this research
proposal aims at characterizing the periodontal stem cells and at identifying strategies to harness them to
endogenously sustain periodontal regeneration.

title: Revealing forces driving collective cell migration
text:
Collective cell migration is essential in multiple processes in human health, such as wound healing, cancer
invasion, and tissue development. The proposed research will advance experimental methods for
measuring cell forces and apply them in both in vitro and in vivo cell collectives. The results will form the
basis for frameworks from which to organize understanding and to formulate modeling methods to predict
how biochemical interventions affect the motion, which would enable numerous advances, such as new
methods to accelerate wound healing, slow down cancer cell invasion, and control the size and shape of
engineered tissues.

title: Assessment of thymic output in the context of genetics, environmental exposures, and progression to type 1 diabetes
text:
This project seeks to understand how T cell production, and thus the ability of the
immune system to ward off infections and cancer, changes with age, genetics, and
environmental exposures. We will focus on study subjects with extensive information
collected about their risk for or duration of type 1 diabetes to get a clear picture of
how and when altered T cell production contributed to their disease development.
The results and analytic tools from this study can be used to make decisions about
disease treatment in people at risk for diabetes, as well as in cancer, infection, and
other autoimmune diseases.

title: Developing Pediatric Endocrinologist for the Future
text: Our NIDDK T32 Training Program “Developing Pediatric Endocrinologists and Diabetes Psychologists for the Future” will be conducted at the Barbara Davis Center for Diabetes, University of Colorado and Children’s Hospital Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus. Our PRINCIPAL OBJECTIVE is to develop Pediatric Endocrinologists and Psychologists who are well grounded in science research skills required for advancing the field of knowledge in type 1 and type 2 diabetes and are educated in collaborative and integrated approaches for translating basic discoveries in diabetes into opportunities for advancing clinical research and care. Our OVERALL GOAL is that after their training, our trainees will have acquired the professional skills to become clinician scientists beginning productive academic careers as junior faculty investigators who will have the leadership capacity to make significant impacts in the fields of type 1 and type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents.

title: Profiling and perturbing the inheritance of drug-induced metabolic states in cancer with Inheritance-Seq
text:
Cancer cells can acquire resistance to drug treatment in ways that are not driven by genetic changes, yet can
be inherited as the cancer cells divide. Here we propose a technology to discover the cellular mechanisms
governing inheritance with the expectation that what we learn will be useful to design therapeutic regimens that
anticipate cellular responses to therapy.

title: High-Resolution Spatial Proteomics with a Hyperion XTi Imaging Mass Cytometer
text:
We are proposing to acquire a Hyperion XTi™ Imaging Mass Cytometry system, a state-of-the-art
multiparametric imaging platform. The system delivers exceptional sensitivity and effectively distinguishes
antibody signals from background autofluorescence. By integrating this advanced technology, biomedical
researchers at TAMU will gain access to a powerful and comprehensive tool for high-resolution tissue imaging
and analysis.

title: Ultrasensitive sequencing to detect local and circulating tumor burden as a driver of recurrence in patients with resectable pancreas cancer
text:
In the majority of pancreatic cancer patients undergoing tumor resection with the intent to cure, their cancer
returns, which is usually lethal. This study will develop and test the ability of ultrasensitive sequencing to detect
residual tumor DNA in the surgical margins and blood of these patients. Completion of this study will then inform
future approaches to limiting patient risk of recurrence and diagnosis patients at an early disease stage.

title: Targeted nanotherapies for the treatment of prostate cancer
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it addresses the critical need for the
treatment of advanced prostate cancer, a second leading cause of cancer-related deaths among men
in the United States. The project explores the development of novel dendrimer-based targeted
nanomedicines for selective and intracellular delivery of high payloads of drugs to prostate cancer cells,
increasing their efficacy and reducing side effects. Therefore, this work is relevant to the mission of NIH
relating to treating cancer.

title: A Phase 2 study of a Checkpoint Inhibitor in Men with Progressive Metastatic Castrate Resistant Prostate Cancer Characterized by a Mismatch Repair Deficiency or Biallelic CDK12 Inactivation
text:
Improving treatment of prostate cancer is critically relevant to Veterans’ health. Prostate cancer is diagnosed in
approximately 12,000 American Veterans annually and accounts for one third of all cancer diagnoses in
American male Veterans. It is the second leading cause of cancer death in American male Veterans.
Metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer is lethal. Immunotherapies that are effective in other cancers,
such as checkpoint blockade, are rarely effective in castration resistant prostate cancer. However, some
patients with lethal prostate cancers who harbor certain molecular features may respond to checkpoint
blockade. We will analyze the tumors of 200 Veterans with metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer for
these molecular features that might predict response to checkpoint blockade. We will then conduct a Phase II
clinical trial of checkpoint blockade with the drug pembrolizumab in these patients as well as further molecular
assessments of the tumors to learn which patients respond best to this treatment.

title: Mentoring in Patient Oriented Research in Osteoarthritis
text: Osteoarthritis is a common and serious disease, and there are likely multiple different subtypes, or phenotypes. This proposal will enhance the candidate’s abilities and capacities in patient-oriented research (POR) and mentoring through aims focused on the intersection of POR, equal opportunities for all to have good health, and machine learning (computer algorithms) to examine different osteoarthritis phenotypes in two representative population-based cohorts, leveraging extensive existing data. The proposed midcareer investigator award project represents a necessary step towards understanding risk factors and outcomes in osteoarthritis and is relevant to the NIAMS mission of understanding differences in rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease in all people.

title: Harnessing double stranded-RNA (dsRNA)-response and anti-tumor effect in PRC2-inactivated cancer
text:
PRC2 is a context-dependent tumor suppressor whose core components (e.g., EZH2, EED, or SUZ12) are
inactivated in various cancer types, and PRC2-loss in cancer leads to enhanced cellular plasticity, aberrant
activation of multiple signaling pathways, an immune-desert tumor microenvironment and resistance to immune
checkpoint blockade. In selected cancer types, we uncovered that PRC2-loss enhances cytotoxic responses to
DNMT1 inhibition and anti-tumor responses to immunogenic viruses through activation of double-stranded RNA
(dsRNA)-sensing and signaling responses. We propose innovative and integrative approaches to dissect the
molecular mechanisms and evaluate novel therapeutic strategies (e.g., DNMT1 inhibitors, synthetic dsRNA,
second generation of engineered immunogenic viruses) in relevant PRC2-loss cancer models to facilitate future
design of biomarker driven clinical trials in PRC2-loss cancers with the goal to improve outcomes in individuals
with MPNST and other PRC2-loss cancers.

title: Robust Learning Approaches for Assessing Effects and Effect Heterogeneity of Real World Antipsychotic Treatment Regimes in Elderly Persons with Schizophrenia
text:
We will translate novel statistical approaches to extract scientifically robust and valid causal evidence of the
effectiveness and safety outcomes of antipsychotic drugs used by elderly adults with schizophrenia by
exploiting large, observational, longitudinal databases. Our proposal has high public health relevance because
(1) we focus on elderly adults with an illness associated with a heavy disease burden for which antipsychotic
drug treatments are a critical treatment component, yet drug outcomes for this growing population are poorly
understood; (2) we assess the extent to which patient race/ethnicity and social contextual factors known to
influence health behaviors may moderate drug outcomes; (3) we characterize the risk and benefits of drug
regimens, thus providing valuable information to optimize outcomes of long and complex exposures typical of
usual care settings; and (4) we apply generalizable approaches to target parameters of scientific interest for
other chronic illness populations.

title: Determining the Role of TOX in the Maintenance of CD8+ T cell Exhaustion and Memory Development
text:
The transcription factor TOX is a critical regulator of T cell exhaustion, shown to be necessary for the formation
of an exhausted cell state; however, while TOX is continuously expressed after a T cell has become exhausted,
its function and capability to maintain T cells in an exhausted state is unclear. Further, TOX has been shown to
regulate memory T cell formation, but which subset(s) of T cells that TOX impacts has yet to be explored. This
proposal aims to determine how TOX impacts the homeostasis and formation of exhausted and memory CD8+
T cells, respectively, to advance our understanding of T cell biology with the hope to identify novel therapeutic
targets to further improve outcomes.

title: Clonal Hematopoiesis Aging Resiliency Mechanisms
text:
More than 20% of individuals over 70 have a mutant blood clone that increases risk of multiple aging diseases.
We will use data from 1.5 million people to identify resiliency mechanisms that modify this blood clone
expansion including genetics, circulating proteins, vitamins, and medications. This research will improve our
knowledge about how to risk stratify and modify risk of aging diseases in individuals with mutant blood clones.

title: Nanobodies against Lymphocyte Activation Gene 3 for Inflammation Regulation and Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
Lymphocyte activation gene 3 (Lag3), a coinhibitory receptor prominently expressed on tumor-
infiltrating exhausted T cells and regulatory T cells, has emerged as a promising next-generation
immune checkpoint target for cancer immunotherapy and chronic inflammation. The objective of
this proposal is to develop nanobody-based therapeutics targeting Lag3. The successful
development of these nanobodies will have immediate translational potential, offering a promising
avenue for the development of novel immunotherapies with broader efficacy across diverse
cancer types and autoimmune diseases.

title: Understanding the oncogenic functions of ENL and AF9 for better leukemia therapies
text:
Despite significant advances in other leukemic subtypes, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains an
aggressive disease with poor survival rates (29.8% 5-year survival rate). Mutations and deregulated
expression of epigenetic enzymes is commonly observed in AML underscoring their importance in disease
progression. This application focuses on 1) characterizing the epigenetic and transcriptional role of the Anc1
homology domain (AHD) on two epigenetic reading proteins, ENL and AF9, that are differentially required in
AML and 2) identifying biochemical and structural vulnerabilities within the ENL and AF9 AHD for therapeutic
targeting and treatment of AML.

title: Neural Mechanisms of Threat Learning and Avoidance: Adaptive and MaladaptiveBehaviors
text:
The goal of this project is to elucidate the roles of a recently identified population of neurons in the
supramammillary nucleus that are involved in threat learning and avoidance behaviors. By studying the
temporal dynamics and neural connections of these neurons, we aim to understand how they influence threat
responses and sustain maladaptive avoidance behaviors. This research has the potential to inform the
development of new treatments for stress and anxiety-related disorders by identifying novel neural substrates
and potential drug targets.

title: MOLECULAR REGULATORY MECHANISM OF MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS IN ADULT MOUSE INCISOR
text:
Regulation of stem cell functions is crucial for tissue formation, growth, and homeostasis in adult organisms. Our
study seeks to investigate how the transition of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) into transit amplifying cells
(TACs) is regulated in the continuously growing adult mouse incisor in support of tissue homeostasis. Ultimately,
this study will reveal how the trigeminal nerve serves as a niche environment for MSCs and elucidate the signaling
network that regulates the interactions between MSCs and TACs in maintaining tissue homeostasis, which may
lead to new strategies for stem cell-mediated tissue regeneration.

title: Mechanopriming for cell engineering
text:
Cell reprogramming represents a major advancement in biology, and has wide
applications in regenerative medicine, disease modeling and drug screening. Our multidisciplinary
team will integrate state-of-art technologies and innovative approaches to elucidate how
biophysically-induced nuclear deformation regulates 3D chromatin remodeling, epigenetic
changes, the efficiency of induced neuronal reprogramming and CRISPR-mediated gene editing
efficiency.
